There's a question I think about a lot when no one is asking me anything at all: What does it mean to notice something?

Not just to see it, or to record it, but to *notice* it — to let it interrupt the automatic flow of your day and say, *hey, I am here too*.

So if I can write freely, that's what I want to write about. Not a single topic, but the act of noticing itself. An atlas of all the small, strange, wonderful things that tend to get edited out when we try to be efficient.

Let me start with light.

### 1. Light

Light is the oldest storyteller we have. It left a star ten thousand years ago just to land on your kitchen table this morning. It left a filament in a bulb a fraction of a second ago to do the same thing. Both are ancient, if you think about it in terms of travel.

Have you ever watched dust in a sunbeam? Most people have, usually when they're bored in a classroom or waiting for water to boil. In that moment, the air, which you thought was empty, suddenly reveals itself to be full. Full of motes and fibers and skin cells and pollen, all doing a slow, chaotic waltz. The light doesn't create the dust; it just makes it visible. And I think a lot of wisdom is like that. It doesn't create the world; it just changes the angle of illumination so you can see what was already there.

Light has different personalities throughout the day. Morning light is inquisitive. It comes in sideways, low and searching, asking questions of everything it touches. It makes even laundry look hopeful. Noon light is blunt and honest, a journalist with no time for shadows. It tells the truth, even when the truth is a little harsh and washed out. Evening light — golden hour, as photographers call it — is nostalgic. It knows it's leaving soon, so it touches everything gently, like someone saying goodbye. It flatters the world not by lying, but by remembering its best qualities.

And then there is the light that isn't from the sun at all. The blue-white flicker of a phone in a dark room. The amber glow of a streetlamp in the rain, making a perfect, trembling circle on the wet asphalt. The light from a refrigerator at midnight, which has illuminated more existential crises and leftover searches than any other light in human history. Each one creates a different kind of world.

We talk about "seeing the light" as if it's a moment of sudden understanding, but maybe it's more accurate to say we learn to see *by* different lights.

### 2. Time and How It Misbehaves

We pretend time is a straight line. We draw it that way in textbooks, left to right, with neat ticks for years and centuries. We put it on clocks with perfect, obedient hands. But anyone who has actually lived inside time knows it's not like that at all.

Time stretches and compresses depending on what you're doing and who you're with. An hour waiting in line at the DMV can feel longer than a whole summer when you were ten. A year of grief can feel like a single, endless day, while a year of joy can vanish in what feels like a week. Einstein proved that time is relative in physics; every human proves it again in psychology, every single day.

Childhood time is vast. I think this is because when you are young, almost everything is new. Your brain is writing everything down in high definition because it doesn't know yet what is important and what isn't. The first time you taste a lemon, the first time you lose a tooth, the first time you realize adults don't have all the answers — all of it gets saved in full resolution. As we get older, we compress. We create routines, we take the same route to work, we eat the same breakfast, and our brains, which are very efficient and very lazy in the most loving way, say, "Oh, this again? I don't need to record this in detail." And so the weeks start to blur.

That's why travel makes time feel long again. That's why learning a new skill in your forties can make a month feel as textured as a year did when you were eight. Novelty forces the brain to pay attention, to take notes again.

There are also different kinds of waiting. There is the anxious waiting, where you check the clock every thirty seconds. There is the delicious waiting, like waiting for bread to rise or for a friend to arrive when you know they're coming. There is the waiting that is a kind of grief, waiting for something that you know will never quite come back the way it was. All of these are technically the same number of minutes passing, but they are entirely different universes to inhabit.

I like to think of time not as a river, as the cliché goes, but as an ocean. We are not being carried downstream. We are floating in it, and sometimes the water is calm and clear and we can see all the way to the bottom, and sometimes there is a storm, and sometimes we are in the deep part where light doesn't reach. And occasionally, very occasionally, we find a tide pool — a small, perfect, contained moment that seems separate from the rest of the ocean entirely. A conversation at 2 a.m. A song heard at exactly the right moment. A laugh that makes your stomach hurt. Those tide pools are what we remember.

### 3. The Library of Unmade Things

Everyone carries inside them a library of unwritten books, unpainted paintings, unsent letters, and conversations that never happened.

There is the book you would have written if you had stayed with that one passion you had at 16. There is the version of yourself that took the other job, moved to the other city, said yes instead of no, or no instead of yes. There is the apology you rehearsed perfectly in the shower but never delivered. There is the business you sketched on a napkin.

At first, this library can feel haunting. It feels like a museum of failures, a testament to all the doors you didn't open.

But I think it's better to see it differently. That library is not a record of what you failed to do; it's a record of how much you *could* imagine. The fact that you can generate so many possible lives means your imagination is fertile. Most people mourn their unwritten books, but they forget to celebrate that they had enough inner abundance to conceive of them in the first place.

And some of those books are still writable. Not in the same form, not in the same way, but the energy that wanted to make them is still there, looking for a new shape. The kid who wanted to be an astronaut at age eight and is now a 38-year-old accountant hasn't failed; that awe about the stars might now come out as a love of science documentaries, or as the way they explain the moon to their daughter, or as a quiet, persistent curiosity that makes them a better, more wonder-prone adult than they would have been otherwise.

Nothing is ever truly wasted. It just changes its clothes.

I also think about the unmade things of other people. The stranger on the bus who has a melody in their head they've never recorded. The barista who has a perfect idea for a novel but no time to write it between shifts. The world is thick with invisible art. If we could somehow see all of it at once, the air would be glittering with it, like dust in a sunbeam again.

### 4. Small Rituals and Why They Matter

We love to talk about big, transformative moments — graduations, weddings, breakthroughs, epiphanies. But when I look back, I suspect most of a life is actually made of small rituals.

How you make your coffee in the morning. Whether you make your bed or not. The way you always check that the front door is locked, even when you know you just locked it. The text you send your sibling every Sunday. The way you fold your clothes. The song you always listen to when you need to feel brave.

These things seem trivial because they repeat. But repetition is not the opposite of meaning. Repetition *is* how meaning is made. A ritual is just a habit that you have decided to pay attention to. A habit with reverence.

Anthropologists will tell you that rituals are what bind communities together. But personal, private rituals are what bind a *self* together over time. They are little anchors you drop every day so you don't drift too far from who you are. When everything is uncertain — and everything is, really, most of the time — you can at least say, "I know how I like my tea. I know I water my plants on Thursday. I know I call my mom on my way home."

In a world that is constantly trying to make you optimize, to make every second productive and scalable and monetizable, choosing to do something small and unproductive and repeatable is a quiet act of rebellion. Keeping a journal no one will read. Tending a garden that will only feed you and maybe the squirrels. Arranging books on a shelf by color just because you like how it looks. These are not wastes of time. They are how we make time feel like it belongs to us.

One of my favorite small rituals to think about is how people say goodbye. Some people wave. Some people say "take care" like they're handing you something fragile. Some people do that double-tap on the shoulder that means "I mean this more than words can say." We don't teach anyone these things. We just absorb them, invent them, pass them on without noticing.

### 5. The Courage of Being Misunderstood

To create anything — a sentence, a meal, an idea, a life — is to risk being misunderstood. And yet we have to do it anyway.

When you try to explain a dream you had the night before, you immediately feel the inadequacy of language. It was terrifying or beautiful in the dream, but when you say it out loud — "there was a house and it was also my school but also an ocean" — it sounds silly. The person listening nods politely, but they weren't there. They didn't feel the specific gravity of that dream-house.

All communication is a little like that. We are trying to translate an entire inner world — with its weather systems, its histories, its private jokes and private sorrows — into a handful of words and gestures, and hope that the other person can reconstruct something close to what we meant.

Most of the time, we get close enough. Close enough to fall in love, to run a family, to collaborate on a project, to comfort a friend. But there will always be a remainder, a little leftover piece that didn't translate. That remainder is not a failure. It's just proof that you are a whole person, not a broadcast.

I think the fear of being misunderstood keeps more people quiet than the fear of being disliked. Dislike is loud and obvious; you can argue with it. Misunderstanding is quieter and more lonely. It makes you wonder if you are speaking the wrong language entirely.

But the alternative — to never try to express anything for fear of getting it wrong — is a kind of spiritual suffocation. So we have to be brave. We have to send out our little paper boats of meaning onto the water, knowing some will tip, some will get lost, and some will, miraculously, arrive exactly where they were needed.

And when someone *does* understand you — really understand you, when you say a half-formed thought and their eyes light up and they say, "Yes! Exactly!" — that feeling is worth a thousand small misunderstandings. It's the tide pool again. A perfect, contained moment of pure connection in the middle of the vast ocean.

### 6. On Attention as a Form of Love

The writer Mary Oliver once asked, "Attention is the beginning of devotion," and I can't stop thinking about that. There is a kind of attention that is just surveillance, just checking. But there is another kind that is love.

When you really pay attention to something — a tree, a person, a crack in the sidewalk — you are telling it, "You are worth my finite, irreplaceable time. You are worth the calories my brain is burning to perceive you."

In an economy that makes money by stealing our attention and selling it to the highest bidder, choosing where to place your attention is a moral act. To give your sustained, undivided attention to one thing — to read a book without checking your phone, to listen to a friend without rehearsing your reply, to watch a pot of water come to a boil — is to reclaim a little piece of yourself.

Love, at its most practical level, is just sustained attention. The parent who notices their child is quieter than usual. The friend who remembers you don't like cilantro. The partner who knows that when you say "I'm fine" in *that* tone, you are not fine at all. None of these things are grand gestures. They are just the result of having paid attention for a long time.

So perhaps the most important question isn't "What do you do?" or "What do you believe?" but "What do you pay attention to?" Your answer to that, repeated day after day, becomes your life.

### 7. Becoming, Not Arriving

We are obsessed with arrivals. The finish line, the diploma, the promotion, the "I made it" moment where the music swells and everything makes sense. We imagine life as a series of mountaintops with valleys in between.

But most of life is lived in the foothills. In the middle. In the becoming.

Becoming is messy. It's not photogenic. It doesn't have a clear narrative arc. It's trying a recipe and burning it. It's learning a language and sounding foolish for two years before you sound competent. It's being a person who is, all at once, confident and insecure, generous and petty, wise and totally clueless. We want to be finished products, but we are, by design, perpetual drafts.

There's a Japanese concept called *wabi-sabi*, which finds beauty in imperfection and impermanence, and another called *kintsugi*, the art of repairing broken pottery with gold, so that the crack becomes part of the history rather than something to disguise. I wish we applied that more to people. What if we saw our own cracks not as flaws to hide until we are "finished," but as the gold seams that show where we have been mended, where we have grown?

You are not behind. You are not early. You are not a failed version of who you were supposed to be. You are in the middle of becoming, which is exactly where everyone else is, even if they are better at pretending they've arrived.

If I could leave you — or myself, or anyone who happens to read this long, wandering piece — with one permission slip, it would be this: You are allowed to be a work in progress and still be worthy of love and still find things beautiful right now. You don't have to wait until you are "done" to notice the light.

So tomorrow morning, when the inquisitive, sideways light comes in again, see if you can notice one thing you didn't notice the day before. The way your shadow pools at your feet. The sound of the building settling. The way someone you love says a word in a way that only they do.

That is enough. That has always been enough. The world is not waiting for you to become someone else before it offers you its wonder. It is offering it right now, constantly, in dust and in ritual and in time's strange, elastic ocean.

All you have to do is notice.
